dimensions.name: Defence & Trade
dimensions.whatThisGrades: Federal action on defence spending and trade diversification away from U.S. reliance.
dimensions.verdictLine: The NATO spending target was met, and Canada's trade is measurably more diversified.
dimensions.status: NATO's 2% target was met, at 2.01%. Trade is measurably more diversified. The U.S. share of Canadian exports fell from 75.9% to 71.7%. The headline grade is driven mainly by the defence side, with trade tracked separately in the sub-scores below.
dimensions.nextTrigger: NATO annual defence spending report (June 2026). CUSMA review (July 2026). Next trade data release.

dimensions.name: Major Projects
dimensions.whatThisGrades: How well the federal system for approving and delivering major infrastructure is working.
dimensions.verdictLine: The Major Projects Office is tracking 15 projects, but only 2 show documented progress so far.
dimensions.status: The Major Projects Office (MPO) is tracking 15 projects in three groups. Four have moved beyond the first stage, called 'designated'. Canada has now started the process to list projects under the Building Canada Act. But only 2 show documented progress after being added to the list. And the government has not yet used its power to declare any project a national-interest project.
dimensions.nextTrigger: First use of the national-interest designation. MPO project completion or cancellation. Alto rail feasibility report.

dimensions.name: Fiscal Health
dimensions.whatThisGrades: Where the federal budget is headed. Can Ottawa keep up its spending and deficit path without it becoming a problem, and do outside watchers find the plan believable?
dimensions.verdictLine: Both fiscal anchors are on track, but rising interest costs and other open worries remain.
dimensions.status: The Spring Economic Update expects a $66.9B deficit for the 2025-26 fiscal year. The PBO (Parliamentary Budget Officer, Parliament's independent fiscal watchdog) says both fiscal anchors (the government's self-set fiscal targets) are on track. Three open worries hold the grade at C: rising interest costs on the debt, how capital spending is labelled, and defence costs that may not all be counted yet.
dimensions.nextTrigger: Next Finance fiscal monitor, any PBO fiscal-anchor update, and Fitch/Moody's/S&P rating actions.

dimensions.name: Economic Policy Response
dimensions.whatThisGrades: Federal action to make Canada's economy more productive and competitive. That means investment, innovation, jobs, and wages.
dimensions.verdictLine: Fewer than two of the core levers are executing, and business investment is still close to flat.
dimensions.status: Canada's weak productivity (how much it gets out of each hour of work) was inherited, not caused by this government. This grade now tracks four kinds of levers the government can pull: tax, trade, regulation, and funding. But fewer than two of the core levers have reached the authorized or executing stage, and business investment is still close to flat.
dimensions.nextTrigger: Treasury Board authorization or first confirmed disbursement for AI compute. Q1 2026 business investment data. Any authorization or disbursement evidence for critical minerals instruments.

dimensions.name: Affordability Response
dimensions.whatThisGrades: How the federal government responds to rising household costs. This covers groceries, costs pushed up by tariffs (taxes on imported goods), and relief aimed at specific groups.
dimensions.verdictLine: Relief measures cover only a small slice of the extra costs families face, and tariffs add more.
dimensions.status: This grade is about what Ottawa did, not about how high world prices are. The relief measures cover only a small slice of the extra costs families face. The Grocery Code is voluntary, so it is weaker than a mandatory rule. And tariffs (taxes on imported goods) are adding to what households pay.
dimensions.nextTrigger: Next monthly CPI release. Any new grocery benefit or mandatory grocery competition measure. Next PROOF food insecurity release.

dimensions.name: Carbon Pricing Policy
dimensions.whatThisGrades: Federal carbon pricing policy. Covers changes to the consumer charge and the industrial system.
dimensions.verdictLine: The consumer carbon price is gone as promised, but the industrial price is weak in practice.
dimensions.status: The consumer carbon price was eliminated, which delivered a campaign promise. Industrial pricing was kept on paper, but the price it actually puts on a tonne of pollution (its effective price) is weak. This grade covers the pricing tool only. The wider climate framework is graded under Climate & Environment.
dimensions.nextTrigger: OBPS tightening schedule or new effective-price evidence. Carbon border adjustment proposal. Broader replacement climate-plan changes remain primary to Climate & Environment.

dimensions.name: Climate & Environment
dimensions.whatThisGrades: Federal climate and environmental policy. How fast emissions are falling, how much nature is protected, and whether the targets still hold.
dimensions.verdictLine: Big environmental rules were rolled back, and Canada is on track for only about half its 2030 target.
dimensions.status: Big environmental rules have been rolled back, with nothing new put in their place. The Canadian Climate Institute (CCI) says Canada is on track to hit only about half the emissions cut its 2030 target requires. For the carbon price on big industrial emitters, see the Carbon Pricing Policy grade.
dimensions.nextTrigger: Government response to CCI February 2026 assessment. Any new climate plan or replacement strategy. ECCC budget execution. OBPS-only pricing changes remain primary to Carbon Pricing Policy.

dimensions.name: Immigration
dimensions.whatThisGrades: Federal immigration policy. This covers how many permanent residents Canada lets in, how many temporary residents are here, and the student and worker streams.
dimensions.verdictLine: The needed immigration correction has been made, but there is still no long-term plan for the system.
dimensions.status: Immigration has been cut sharply. The correction is big and was needed, and the temporary-resident share is now down to about 6.18% of the population. But there is still no long-term plan for how the system should run. That plan is the main thing being watched for the next grade move.
dimensions.nextTrigger: Next quarterly population estimate (StatsCan). IRCC monthly data. Healthcare staffing data showing pullback impact.

dimensions.name: Housing Supply
dimensions.whatThisGrades: Whether federal housing policy is getting homes delivered at the scale Canada needs.
dimensions.verdictLine: Federal housing programs are not yet big enough, and announced homes have not started construction.
dimensions.status: Federal housing programs are not yet big enough to meet the need. Build Canada Homes is now legislated, but announced homes have still not started construction, and housing starts are running below the pace needed to close the gap (the shortfall).
dimensions.nextTrigger: Next CMHC monthly starts release. Actual Build Canada Homes construction commencement. Signed Ontario BCSF / DCRP agreement, first payment, or construction evidence.

dimensions.name: Ethics & Transparency
dimensions.whatThisGrades: Whether the Prime Minister's ethics setup is strong enough for someone with his money and career history.
dimensions.verdictLine: Nothing wrong has been proven, but the ethics setup is missing pieces and the disclosure gap is open.
dimensions.status: The ethics setup is missing pieces that a background like his calls for. Nothing wrong has been proven. The gap in what has been disclosed is still open.
dimensions.nextTrigger: Ethics Commissioner publication of Brookfield review. Any new disclosure of retained financial interests. House Ethics Committee report.

dimensions.name: Flagship Delivery
dimensions.whatThisGrades: A combined delivery score pulled from five of the government's biggest areas: defence, housing, major projects, climate, and immigration. This grade is built from those five, not judged on its own.
dimensions.verdictLine: Defence and immigration are getting done, while housing, major projects, and climate are stalled.
dimensions.status: Defence and immigration are clearly getting done. Housing, major projects, and climate are stalled, meaning no measurable progress yet or progress has stopped after initial action.
dimensions.nextTrigger: Post-majority legislative pace (bills passed per month). First Ministers Meeting outcomes. April 28 economic update implementation.

dimensions.name: Promise Delivery
dimensions.whatThisGrades: A running tracker of specific things the government promised to do. Each one is marked delivered, in progress, stalled, or abandoned.
dimensions.status: Fiscal-anchor delivery, meaning progress against the government's own budget rules, is back in progress, but housing and climate promises still fall short.
dimensions.nextTrigger: Next major policy announcement or delivery milestone. Housing starts trajectory. Climate replacement strategy if any.
